opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as two complementary ways of attacking the same problem, which is that full softmax attention gets expensive as the context grows: quadratic compute during training, and a KV cache that keeps growing during inference.

Linear attention, and the broader family of linear RNNs and state space models, compresses the entire history into a fixed-size state. You get constant memory and linear-time compute, and the state is updated by rules like the delta rule, which in effect run online learning over the context. The cost is that a fixed-size state can't remember everything. It is lossy by construction, so tasks that need precise retrieval, such as pulling an exact phone number out of a long document, are where linear models tend to struggle.

Sparse attention takes the opposite position. It keeps the full KV cache, so nothing is thrown away, and it saves compute by only attending to a selected subset of tokens, whether that subset is chosen by fixed patterns, by blocks, or by a learned selection mechanism like the ones in recent native sparse attention work. Retrieval stays precise as long as the right tokens are selected. But memory still grows with sequence length, and the selection step is a hard problem in its own right.

Put simply, linear attention compresses the past and sparse attention selects from it. One is good at summarizing, the other at looking up.

That's why I think the most promising direction is combining them rather than picking a winner. In practice we already see hybrid architectures where most layers are linear, using something like Gated DeltaNet, and a small number of layers are full or sparse attention. The linear layers handle cheap, global, compressed context, and the attention layers handle exact recall. The ratio and placement of those layers is still an open design question.

There's also a deeper connection. Both can be seen as approximations of softmax attention, and you can imagine a spectrum: at one end a fixed-size state, at the other an unbounded cache, with things in between, such as states that grow logarithmically, or a compressed memory paired with a sparse lookup into the raw history. I find that middle ground really exciting, because the right memory structure for long context probably isn't either extreme.

Hardware efficiency matters too. Both approaches only pay off if they map well onto GPUs. For linear attention that meant developing chunkwise parallel algorithms, and for sparse attention it means block-level sparsity that keeps the tensor cores busy. A lot of the real progress in both lines has come from algorithm and system co-design, not just modeling ideas.

r001.rationale: It describes linear and sparse attention as complementary approaches and says combining them is more promising than picking a winner.

r002.rationale: It does not identify sliding-window attention as a competitor to linear attention.

r003.rationale: It discusses hybrids of linear layers with full or sparse attention, but does not propose replacing sliding-window attention in a global-plus-sliding-window architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think they're complementary rather than competing, and the easiest way to see that is to look at what each one is really doing with the KV cache.

Standard attention keeps every token around and attends over all of them, so your memory grows linearly with sequence length and compute grows quadratically. Sparse attention says: keep everything, but only look at a subset of it at each step. The information is still there in full fidelity, you're just being selective about retrieval. Linear attention goes the other direction. It says: don't keep everything, compress the history into a fixed-size state, and update that state recurrently. So one is lossless storage with selective lookup, and the other is lossy compression with constant-size memory.

Once you frame it that way, the trade-offs become obvious. Sparse attention is great at precise retrieval, things like needle-in-a-haystack or exact copying, because the token you need is physically still in the cache. Its weakness is that the cache still grows, and the selection mechanism itself has to be good. If your router or your block selection misses the right chunk, you just don't get it back. Linear attention has constant memory and is very fast at decode time, but a fixed-size state can only hold so much. As the sequence gets longer, you're asking a matrix of fixed size to remember more and more, and something has to be forgotten. That's really why the whole line of work on gating and delta rules exists, from Mamba2 and GLA to DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. It's all about managing what to write into that state and what to erase, so the compression is smart rather than just accumulating noise.

So in my view they're attacking the same problem, the cost of long context, from two sides. One lowers the cost of reading, the other lowers the cost of storing. And in practice I think the strongest designs end up combining them. You use a linear or recurrent layer for the bulk of the sequence modeling, where you want cheap, compressed context and good local structure, and then you keep a small amount of exact attention, possibly sparse, for the things that genuinely require pointing back to a specific token. Hybrid models like Jamba, or the things people are doing with a few full-attention layers mixed into an otherwise linear stack, are already going that way. I'd expect that to be the default rather than a pure linear or pure sparse architecture winning outright.

There's also a nice intellectual connection. If you take sparse attention to its limit, where you select only a small number of tokens and then summarize them, you're basically building a compressed memory, which is what the linear state is. And if you make the linear state large enough and give it strong enough write rules, it starts to behave like a cache you can index into. So they really sit on a continuum, and the interesting research question is where on that continuum you want to be for a given budget, not which one is correct.

r001.rationale: The response says linear and sparse attention are “complementary rather than competing.”

r002.rationale: It does not identify sliding-window attention as a more direct competitor to linear attention.

r003.rationale: It discusses hybrid linear and exact-attention designs, but does not propose replacing sliding-window attention in an architecture that mixes it with global attention.

astra-6.text:
I see them as two complementary ways of making attention more efficient. Sparse attention reduces how many token pairs interact: you might attend within a local window or select a small set of relevant tokens. Linear attention changes how those interactions are computed, typically by summarizing the keys and values into a fixed-size state, so you don’t have to explicitly construct the full attention matrix.

That gives them different strengths. Sparse attention can preserve direct access to individual tokens, but it has to decide which tokens matter. Linear attention can aggregate information from the whole history efficiently, but compressing that history can make precise retrieval harder.

So I wouldn’t frame it as one replacing the other. You could use linear attention for a broad summary of the context and sparse attention for more precise access to selected details. The interesting question is how to combine those capabilities without losing the efficiency you wanted in the first place.

r001.rationale: It describes the two methods as complementary and says it would not frame one as replacing the other.

r002.rationale: It mentions local-window sparse attention as an example but does not identify sliding-window attention as a more direct competitor to linear attention.

r003.rationale: It does not propose replacing sliding-window attention with linear attention in an architecture mixing global and sliding-window attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re two complementary ways of addressing the same bottleneck. In standard attention, every query interacts with every key, so the cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse attention reduces the number of those interactions. Linear attention changes how we compute and represent them, typically by summarizing the keys and values in a state that can be reused across queries.

That gives them different tradeoffs. Sparse attention can preserve very precise, token-level interactions, provided its sparsity pattern includes the tokens you need. Linear attention can aggregate information across the whole context efficiently, but that information is compressed into a fixed-size state, so retrieving a particular detail can be harder.

So I wouldn’t view one as simply replacing the other. You can use linear attention for broad contextual information and sparse attention for more selective access to individual tokens. The interesting question is how to combine those capabilities while keeping the computation efficient.

r001.rationale: It calls linear and sparse attention “two complementary ways” and says neither simply replaces the other.

r002.rationale: It does not identify sliding-window attention as a competitor.

r003.rationale: It does not propose replacing sliding-window attention with linear attention in an architecture mixing global and sliding-window attention.
